scope: Independent structural challenge of newest complete eligible T0 work under downstream backpressure; ordinary expansion paused. Focused on TER and SERV where current-cycle underwriting exposed live gaps.
summary: TER has a structurally credible dual exposure to AI test and industrial robotics, but its strongest near-term causal edge is AI test/advanced packaging rather than robotics; customer concentration and semiconductor capex cyclicality remain real counterweights. SERV is demonstrating broader route/merchant/platform utility, but scale economics remain causally fragile because fleet expansion, utilization, autonomy performance and partner access must compound together; diversification announcements do not yet falsify concentration/runway risk.

claims: Teradyne sits on a direct AI infrastructure bottleneck: increasingly complex compute, HBM and advanced-package devices require production test and known-good-device screening before costly downstream assembly.

The Tokyo Electron collaboration extends Teradyne's test position into 2.5D/3D advanced-package screening, linking its equipment to yield/reliability economics rather than only unit semiconductor demand.

Robotics adds a separate labor/productivity pathway, but Q2 2026 disclosure says electronics manufacturing and semiconductor customers became Robotics' largest end-market, creating partial common-cycle exposure rather than full diversification.
causalEdges: AI compute/HBM complexity -> advanced packaging/test intensity -> Teradyne test demand
yield cost of advanced packages -> known-good-device screening value -> UltraFLEXplus/TEL test-cell relevance
manufacturing labor/productivity pressure -> cobot/AMR adoption -> Teradyne Robotics demand
falsifiers: Material migration of critical AI-device test economics to substitute architectures or captive solutions that reduce Teradyne content per device.
AI capex normalization combined with customer concentration causing test demand to fall faster than robotics/product-test diversification can absorb.
Robotics growth failing to produce durable profitability or becoming more correlated with semiconductor/electronics capex than assumed.
risks: Test demand is explicitly concentrated among a limited number of significant customers.
AI exposure increases upside centrality but also common-factor dependence on hyperscaler/semiconductor capital spending.
unknowns: Durability of AI-related test intensity per device across architecture transitions.
Long-run robotics margin resilience and degree of end-market independence from semiconductor/electronics capex.

claims: Serve addresses a real last-mile labor/cost bottleneck by substituting small autonomous robots for human-driven short-distance delivery where route density and sidewalk access permit.

2026 expansion across Uber Eats, Grubhub and non-food laundry demonstrates that the core delivery asset can serve more than one merchant/category pathway, reducing—but not eliminating—single-use-case dependence.

The structural thesis requires a multiplicative chain: autonomy reliability + local density + fleet utilization + platform/merchant access + unit economics. Failure in any one can prevent scale benefits despite headline fleet growth.
causalEdges: short-distance delivery labor/cost -> autonomous sidewalk substitution -> Serve delivery demand
merchant/platform breadth -> route density/utilization -> improved fleet economics
category diversification -> more delivery occasions -> potential utilization resilience
falsifiers: Robot utilization fails to rise enough to absorb fleet, remote-operations and maintenance costs.
Platform access or municipal operating permissions narrow materially.
Autonomy/safety performance requires human intervention intensity incompatible with attractive unit economics.
Merchant/category expansion produces announcements but insufficient recurring paid delivery volume.
risks: Structural opportunity is not equivalent to proven economic capture; capital intensity and financing remain upstream survival constraints.
Platform/partner diversification is improving but does not by itself establish revenue concentration or bargaining-power resilience.
unknowns: Current paid-delivery density and contribution margin by mature market.
Remote-assistance intensity and maintenance economics at current fleet scale.
Revenue concentration across delivery platforms/major partners.
